description: Hi everyone! 🚀 We are students from UDEM, Mexico, excited to participate in NASA Space Apps Challenge again! We're enthusiastic, curious, and passionate about space, science, and innovation. We're looking for motivated teammates with diverse skills in programming, design, science, or data analysis who love teamwork, sharing ideas, and solving challenges creatively. Let's learn, innovate, and have fun together!
summary: Expedition Mars: The Great Rover Crisis is an educational web game and printable kit that tells the story of NASA’s discarded equipment on Mars. Players are astronauts who crash near Utopia Planitia in the year 2036 and must travel through seven real Mars locations to rebuild their ship using parts from Spirit, Viking 1, Opportunity, Ingenuity, InSight, Phoenix and Viking 2. At each stop they read NASA-based descriptions, explore each machine’s real instruments, learn how its mission ended, and complete repair mini-games. A fictional storyline keeps the adventure exciting, while all equipment information is real and sourced from NASA. Our project answers the challenge by making forgotten hardware the hero of the story. It matters because the history of space exploration is scattered and technical, so it rarely reaches children and young people. We turn that legacy into an experience that sparks curiosity about space science.
details:
Expedition Mars is a browser game for PC, laptop, phone or tablet, set in 2036. A mysterious electromagnetic wave makes the player’s ship crash in Gusev Crater, and the only way forward is a locked route through seven real Mars locations. At each stop the player reads a NASA-based description of the place, examines the machine left there, opens its real instruments one by one, and reads its “last report” and mission-control message, which explain how its mission ended (for example, dust covering the solar panels of Opportunity and InSight). Four of the machines provide a ship part, repaired through a mini-game (cleaning dust, tuning an antenna, digging, a liftoff maze). A final battle closes the story, with three difficulty modes for mouse, trackpad and touch-screen players.

Players learn where each machine landed, what instruments it carried and why it went silent, without reading a technical report. We want to spark curiosity in school-age explorers and show that retired space hardware still has stories and science to share.

Beyond the screen. Not everything has to be digital. The project includes a printable Mars Rescue Mission kit: a mission board, cut-out robots, a rocket to build, a checklist, a storyteller guide and an explorer certificate. It encourages hands-on learning, creativity and manual skills, works in classrooms without devices, and promotes STEAM and space sciences.

The content (locations, equipment, instruments, last reports) is organized as editable data, so the same design can be reused with other worlds and missions, such as equipment left on the Moon or on other planets. It can serve as a learning tool for any set of “forgotten” machines.

Tools. HTML, CSS and JavaScript, written with the help of AI assistants (Claude and Google Gemini) to generate, decode and debug code, and published on Wix. Canva for the presentation and visual materials, Google tools for research, and NASA mission pages and images for the content.

Creativity and factors considered. The machines are the heroes, and their last messages tell the story. The plot (the interference and the final battle) is fiction, while the equipment information is real, and the game says so clearly. We considered accuracy against NASA sources, age-appropriate language, different devices and input methods, and offline use through printing.

Use of SI. We used AI assistants (Claude, Google Gemini) for coding and debugging, research support, translation and editing, illustrations for the printable materials, The idea, story and design decisions are our own, and facts were checked against NASA pages.
